claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal phase or colony boundaries produce localized stress concentrations in the untreated alloy.
The localized stress concentrations promote premature microcrack nucleation and brittle failure during straining.
A short post-solidification anneal just below the eutectic temperature will induce mild compositional segregation at internal interfaces.
The anneal will locally reconfigure lamellar colony boundaries.
Interfacial segregation and boundary reconfiguration will create thin, ductile interfacial films.
The ductile interfacial films will act as bridges that facilitate dislocation transfer across phases.
Facilitating dislocation transfer will alleviate dislocation pile-ups at lamellar colony boundaries.
Alleviating dislocation pile-ups will reduce localized stress concentrations and premature microcrack nucleation.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the annealed alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature elongation to failure.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the annealed alloy will maintain or modestly increase yield strength.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the annealed alloy will maintain or modestly increase ultimate tensile strength.
A treatment duration of approximately 10–30 minutes below the eutectic temperature is proposed, with rapid quenching if necessary.
Keeping the annealing temperature below the eutectic point will maintain the primary phases.
Excessive annealing could cause phase coarsening or loss of strength.
The proposed benefit is intended for room-temperature tensile loading in air at standard strain rates.
